nameStory: The Cyrano Darner gets its distinctive name from its dramatically long, pointed face projection that resembles the famous large nose of Cyrano de Bergerac, the fictional French swordsman and poet. This prominent "nose" is actually an extension of the frons (the front part of the dragonfly's head) that makes this species instantly recognizable. Like its literary namesake, this dragonfly carries its distinctive feature with unmistakable flair.
description: The Cyrano Darner is a large, impressive dragonfly that patrols New England's wetlands with powerful, direct flight. Adults reach about 3 inches long with a wingspan of nearly 4 inches, making them one of our more substantial dragonflies. They have the typical darner build - long, slender bodies with strong, clear wings - but sport distinctive brownish-green coloration rather than the bright blues and greens of many other darners. Most notably, they have an unmistakable pointed projection extending forward from their face, giving them an almost comical profile when viewed from the side.

idTips.label: Pointed face projection
idTips.description: A distinctive horn-like projection extends forward from the front of the head, visible in profile like a pointed beak or nose - no other New England dragonfly has this feature

idTips.label: Brown-green coloration
idTips.description: Overall brownish-green body coloration with darker markings, lacking the bright blues and emerald greens typical of most other darner species

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Substantial dragonfly about 3 inches long that flies with powerful, steady wingbeats rather than the more erratic flight of smaller species

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely clear without the amber or colored patches seen in some other large dragonflies, making a distinct rustling sound in flight

idTips.label: Patrol behavior
idTips.description: Flies in regular patrol patterns along shorelines and over open water, often returning to the same perching spots on emergent vegetation

habitat: Cyrano Darners prefer larger freshwater habitats including ponds, lakes, and slow-moving sections of rivers and streams, especially those with abundant emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They're most commonly found in areas with muddy or silty bottoms where their nymphs can burrow, and they favor waters surrounded by mixed forest rather than completely open areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with peak emergence in early June. Fresh individuals can be identified by their pristine wings and more vibrant coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to observe their characteristic patrol flights and pointed face projection.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into September and sometimes early October, though individuals become less common and more worn-looking with tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent; nymphs overwinter underwater in the muddy bottom sediments of their aquatic habitats, taking 2-3 years to develop.

funFact: Cyrano Darner nymphs are incredibly patient hunters that can remain motionless buried in mud for weeks at a time, with only their eyes and the tip of their breathing tube exposed - they're like underwater snipers waiting for the perfect moment to ambush passing prey.
confusionNotes: The pointed face projection makes mature Cyrano Darners nearly impossible to confuse with other species, but distant or quick glimpses might be confused with other large brown darners like the Swamp Darner - remember "Cyrano's nose" as your key identifying feature and look for that distinctive profile.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "darner" like other members of this family, the name doesn't refer to darning needles or sewing - it's an old folk belief that dragonflies could sew up people's ears or mouths, though of course they're completely harmless to humans.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England, the Cyrano Darner is most easily compared to other large darners in the Aeshna genus like the Common Green Darner or Swamp Darner. However, none of these relatives have the distinctive pointed face projection, and most display much brighter blue or green coloration rather than the Cyrano's subdued brownish-green tones.
